deed: ססר מילשטיין פיתח שיטה לייצור נוגדנים חד-שבטיים וזכה בנובל לרפואה 1984
title: César Milstein, son of a Jewish immigrant, found a way to produce antibodies in large quantities and won the Nobel Prize in Medicine

trailer.text: César Milstein, a scientist born in Bahía Blanca, Argentina, and the son of a Jewish immigrant father, is one of the three winners of the 1984 Nobel Prize in Medicine.
Before his work, scientists struggled to produce large amounts of a single antibody, because the cells that produce antibodies were difficult to grow in the laboratory.
In 1975, in Cambridge, Milstein and Georges Köhler developed a method to combine tumor cells with antibody-producing cells, in order to produce antibodies of the same type.
The combined cell, called a hybridoma, could produce antibodies continuously.

Monoclonal antibody production was one of the driving forces in the creation of the biotechnology industry, and according to the MRC institute, monoclonal antibodies today account for at least a third of all new treatments against a range of diseases.

paragraphs.text: César Milstein was born on October 8, 1927, in Bahía Blanca, Argentina.
He was the middle of three sons, born to a Jewish immigrant father and a mother who was a teacher.
His father came from Ukraine to Argentina alone, as a teenager.
As a child he was drawn to science after reading about microbe hunters such as van Leeuwenhoek and Pasteur.
He studied at the University of Buenos Aires, where he completed a PhD on the enzyme aldehyde dehydrogenase.
In 1953 he married Celia, who was also an immunologist.
Milstein was proud of his Jewish heritage.
In 1958 he travelled to Britain to work in the Biochemistry Department of the University of Cambridge.
There he received a second PhD.

According to The Irish Times, Milstein returned to Argentina in 1961, and two years later, when dozens of faculty members were dismissed following the military coup, he resigned his job and went back to Cambridge.
According to AAI, he was frustrated by political interference in his laboratory after the 1962 coup, and returned to Cambridge in 1963.
At the suggestion of Frederick Sanger, Milstein moved from enzyme research to immunology.

stations.title: The problem: one antibody, in quantity

paragraphs.text: The human immune system can produce more than two million different antibodies.

According to the MRC institute, the ability of antibodies to bind specifically is very useful for medical research, but it was difficult to produce large quantities of specific antibodies in the laboratory.
The difficulty was growing the antibody-producing B cells in culture.
These cells were easy to harvest from the spleens of mice, but in laboratory culture they grew only briefly.
On the other hand, the researchers had myeloma cells, a cancer that grows in the laboratory without limit and produces immunoglobulin.

stations.title: The idea: fuse two cells into one

paragraphs.text: Georges Köhler arrived in Cambridge in 1974.
Together with Milstein, he sought to use cell fusion to create an antibody-secreting cell line.
According to the Irish Times, the two decided to fuse tumor cells of the immune system, myelomas, with B cells that produce antibodies.
The combined cell was called a hybridoma.
It had infinite life and could produce antibodies continuously.
According to the MRC institute, the fused cells were collected and cloned.
In this way, in 1975, the hybridoma technique for the production of monoclonal antibodies was developed.
The paper describing the method was published in Nature that same year.
After the publication, Köhler returned to Basel.
Milstein worked for several years with Giovanni Galfré to show that monoclonal antibodies could be used.
Galfré introduced Sendai virus as the fusing agent, thereby improving the process and making it more reliable.
The technique spread quickly to research institutes around the world, and was used, among other things, for grouping blood types.
According to the MRC institute, Milstein's work transformed the field of immunology and revealed new insights into the structure, function and diversity of antibodies.
He also solved the puzzle of affinity maturation, the process by which antibodies change their sequences to improve their efficacy.
At first, therapeutic use was limited, because the antibodies provoked a cross-species immune response.
According to the LMB institute, it took about 20 years until the approach was applied to humans, following research led by Greg Winter and Michael Neuberger.
Humira, the first fully human monoclonal antibody drug, was launched in 2003 to treat rheumatoid arthritis.
Today, monoclonal antibodies are used to treat diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis, multiple sclerosis, some forms of cancer and viral infections.
According to AAI, the greatest impact is in oncology, where monoclonal antibodies that bind to tumors are being developed.
The 1984 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine was awarded jointly to Niels Jerne, Georges Köhler and César Milstein.
The prize was given for theories concerning the specificity in development and control of the immune system, and for the discovery of the principle for production of monoclonal antibodies.
Jerne, a Danish scientist, developed the theories of the immune system that Milstein and Köhler went on to develop.
According to AAI, Köhler had formerly been Milstein's postdoctoral fellow.
In his acceptance speech, Milstein stressed that the hybridoma technology was an unexpected by-product of basic research to understand the immune system.
Abraham Karpas wrote that Milstein's contribution is the most important immunological advance of the century.
In 1984 Milstein also won the Lasker Award for creating the first hybridomas.
In addition to the Nobel, he won the Wolf Prize in Medicine and the Louisa Gross Horwitz Prize from Columbia University.
In 1975 he was elected a Fellow of the Royal Society, and in 1989 he received the Copley Medal.
In 1995 Milstein became a Companion of Honour, and in 2000 he received the Presidential Medal of Merit for Scientific Excellence from Argentina.
According to the AAI, in 1983 Milstein was named head of the Protein and Nucleic Acid Chemistry Division of the MRC, a position he held until his retirement in 1995.
He retired in the mid-1990s.
He received British citizenship and held dual citizenship, British and Argentine.
He helped science and scientists in developing countries.
Milstein died on March 24, at the age of 74.
In 2003 the LMB institute held a memorial meeting in his name.
The Milstein Studentship funds Argentine PhD students so that they can complete their studies at the LMB.
In 2010 a documentary film about his life was released.

According to The Irish Times, there was some regret in the 1980s when it was found that the British government's National Research Development Corporation had decided not to attempt to patent the hybridoma technology.
According to the History & Policy website, the NRDC declined to patent the work after Milstein submitted it for consideration.
